analysis.one_liner: Requires health plans to cover emergency room care at in-network cost without prior approval, under a 'prudent layperson' standard.
analysis.headline: With 104 cosponsors from both parties, the bill to guarantee emergency care coverage was sent to three House committees and subcommittees and never received a hearing or vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill said that if a health plan covers emergency services at all, it must cover them whenever a typical person would reasonably think it was an emergency — no advance permission required, no penalty for landing at a hospital outside the plan's network, and no bill bigger than the in-network share. It applied to employer plans and individual insurance, and required plans to tell members annually how emergency coverage works. It was referred to three House committees, sent down to subcommittees, and never came back out.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with employer-based or individual health insurance who might one day need an emergency room: the bill removed the financial risk of being charged out-of-network prices for care they could not choose, and stopped insurers from denying emergency claims afterward because the diagnosis turned out not to be an emergency. People in plans with narrow networks or strict authorization rules had the most to gain.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Insured workers and families facing ER bills

how_it_helps.text: It defined an emergency by the 'prudent layperson' test: what an average person with severe pain or acute symptoms would reasonably think needs immediate care, so coverage no longer hinged on how a final diagnosis turned out.
It barred plans from requiring prior approval before emergency care, so a person in crisis would not wait for a phone call to a plan's hotline.
It capped what a patient could be billed when the nearest emergency room was out of the plan's network, capping their liability at what an in-network visit would have cost them.

It required plans to pay non-network providers for follow-up and post-stabilization care at the same rate as network providers, and to give enrollees annual written information on how to get and pay for emergency care.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and, through them, employers who fund group plans, would have borne higher claims costs from covering out-of-network emergency visits and paying non-network providers for post-stabilization care, with some of the cost likely passed to premiums.
analysis.who_pays_short: Health insurers and employer plan sponsors

drawbacks.text: Covering out-of-network emergency care at in-network cost-sharing and reimbursing non-network post-stabilization care would raise claims costs for health insurers and employers, and some of that cost would likely be passed back to workers as higher premiums.

The bill applied no fee schedule of its own, so out-of-network emergency providers could bill plans at higher rates; plans and patients could still face disputes over what counts as a reasonable payment, and the bill did not create a neutral process for resolving them.
The prudent layperson standard is inherently a judgment call, which critics said could invite more emergency department use for non-urgent problems and add cost without improving care.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: On its merits, the bill offered a clear consumer protection at a modest, bounded cost: it did not mandate new coverage, only limited how plans could deny or charge for care a person reasonably believed was an emergency. The main trade-off is higher claims costs for insurers and employers, which could feed into premiums, and some pressure on emergency departments already serving as care of last resort. Those costs are real but narrow compared with the financial risk the bill removed for patients. It died without a hearing or vote anyway, so no weighing of amendments or design flaws ever occurred in public.

outcome.mechanism: The House referred the bill to three committees, each committee passed it down to a health subcommittee, and nothing ever came back out, so it never got a hearing or a vote before the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 2, 1999 and referred to the Commerce, Education and Workforce, and Ways and Means committees.
Within a month it had been referred to three subcommittees: Health (Commerce), Health and Environment, and Employer-Employee Relations.
No further action was recorded for the rest of the 106th Congress, which ended January 3, 2001.
The bill had accumulated 104 cosponsors across both parties, far more than the support typically needed to clear a committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers kept their ability to deny or underpay emergency claims through prior authorization and network rules; employers bore no new compliance costs. Working people kept bearing surprise out-of-network emergency bills until a similar standard was enacted years later.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers kept denying emergency claims

for.name: Ben Cardin
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and gathered a broad bipartisan group of original cosponsors.

for.name: 104 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, signaling support well beyond the sponsor's party.

for.name: House leadership and committee chairs (Commerce, Education and the Workforce, Ways and Means)
for.role: Committee and subcommittee gatekeepers in the 106th Congress
for.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to a markup or floor vote; it sat in subcommittee referral for the entire two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Sponsorship was bipartisan — 104 cosponsors including 32 Republicans and 71 Democrats — and the bill died in committee rather than on a party-line vote.

industries.note: The bill would have removed their most common tools for limiting emergency claims: prior authorization, network restrictions, and charging patients the difference for out-of-network ER visits. It died, so they kept them.

Employers sponsoring plans would bear compliance requirements and potentially higher claims costs, though the bill let plans satisfy the mandate through their insurer. Most employer plans could pass costs to workers through premiums.

industries.industry: Hospital emergency departments and emergency physicians
industries.note: Emergency providers were often left uncompensated when plans refused claims after the fact; guaranteed coverage would have made ER care reliably billable. These providers are also the channel through which uninsured and insured people alike get emergency care.
